description: Trametes versicolor (Turkey Tail) is an extremely common, cosmopolitan bracket fungus forming thin, leathery, fan-shaped caps with concentric, multicolored zones and a finely velvety upper surface. The underside bears a layer of tiny white pores. It grows in overlapping clusters and rosettes on dead hardwood and is widely used in traditional medicine.
edibilityNotes: Not edible as food: the fruiting body is thin, tough, leathery and indigestible. It is consumed only as a decoction (tea) or as standardized extracts. The polysaccharide-K (PSK/krestin) extract is used as an adjuvant cancer therapy in Japan and PSP is studied in China; do not treat this as general culinary edibility. The mushroom itself is not toxic.
distribution: Cosmopolitan; found throughout temperate forests worldwide, including North America, Europe, and Asia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Stereum ostrea (False Turkey Tail)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Not dangerous, but commonly confused. Lacks pores: its underside is smooth, not porous. Turkey Tail has a distinct layer of tiny white pores (roughly 3-8 per mm) underneath. Checking for pores is the key ID step before brewing tea.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Trichaptum biforme (Violet-toothed Polypore)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Not dangerous, but a frequent lookalike. Underside is purplish and toothed/jagged rather than white with fine round pores; the violet tone fades with age but the irregular, toothed hymenophore distinguishes it.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Trametes hirsuta (Hairy Bracket)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Not dangerous. Coarser, conspicuously hairy grayish-white zones with less vivid coloration; pores generally larger and the surface shaggier.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Trametes ochracea
dangerousLookalikes.note: Not dangerous. Thicker, more bunched zones with browner/ochre tones; less thin and less vividly multicolored than true Turkey Tail.
